Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Canadian National Railway Company may construct and complete terminal stations and facilities and other railway works and improvements at or in the vicinity of the city of Montreal, and the governor in council may guarantee the principal and interest of securities to be issued for these purposes by the company
[Mr. Geary.1
to an amount not exceeding $50,000,000, and the proceeds of any sale, pledge or disposition of the securities shall be deposited to the credit of the Minister of Finance in trust for the company, and released from time to time to the company by the said minister to be applied to expenditures made or indebtedness incurred in connection with the said works.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

I think at would be well for me to make a brief general statement regarding what is contemplated as a result of this resolution, although necessarily, in dealing with a matter so large, as was indicated during the discussion on the last resolution, it will be desirable for the proper committee of the house to go very carefully into the proposal in all its bearings, into all the plans of what is proposed and generally into the manner of dealing with it.
One of the many problems with which the Canadian National railway management has been faced in the development of that system has centred around the city of Montreal, a particularly important railway centre. The problem is not a new one; it has for some years engaged the attention not only of the present management of the national railways, but of previous managements of the constituent parts of the system, as well as the city council and the citizens of Montreal. Prior to the war the Grand Trunk Railway Company, in conjunction with the city and the Board of Railway Commissioners, had made a study of the situation affecting principally the separation of grades between Bonaventure station and Victoria bridge and Turcot, and had developed a plan involving the raising of the tracks of the railway company in this area to a sufficient extent to permit vehicular traffic to pass underneath the railway facilities. This plan involved the construction of a new passenger station upon the site of Bonaventure station. The estimated cost of the project at that time before the War, was 815,300,000, and when the government acquired the Grand Trunk, it was considered as a capital expenditure which would have to be faced in time, the then estimated cost, due to advancing prices, being slightly over $20,000,000.
The Canadian Northern Railway Company, through its subsidiary the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company, broke ground in June, 1912, in connection with the construction of a tunnel entrance to the city. The work was in progress at the time the Canadian Northern railway system was taken over by the Dominion government in 1918, and shortly before the end of the war the tunnel was

C.N.R.-.1/ontreal Terminal
opened for traffic, the first train 'being oper~ ated into the tunnel station on Lagauchetiere street on October 28, 1918. In connection with the general plan of this Canadian Northern entrance, considerable property was acquired between the tunnel station * at Lagauchetiere street and the harbour front for the purpose of extension to the harbour tracks, but because of the financial situation of the Canadian Northern and the evident necessity of coordinating these terminal facilities with those of the Grand Trunk Railway, the acquisition of which was under negotiation by the government in 1918, the completion of this work was halted and the situation remains exactly the same to-day as it did then. During the war and the period immediately after the war, public agitation for improved conditions naturally died down in spite of the fact that grade crossing difficulties and terminal congestion due to the constantly increasing traffic both in the railway terminals and on the city streets crossing the railway tracks, became more and more acute.
When Sir Henry Thornton took charge of the administration of the Canadian National Railways, public agitation for an improvement in the situation had again developed, and steps were initiated to study the situation from the Canadian National point of view. It soon became evident to Sir Henry Thornton and his officers that the expenditure involved in a readjustment of the terminal facilities would be very large, and also that the financial position of the Canadian National at that time would hardly justify the immediate assumption of the capital load involved. Studies were continued with a view to developing the most satisfactory plan from the point of view of the Canadian National Railways. Meanwhile the conditions affecting the operation of the Canadian National Railway traffic at Montreal became so acute because of interference with vehicular traffic at the numerous grade crossings, that it became evident that the problem required to be speedily dealt with. Accordingly, as Minister of Railways, on the advice of the management of the Canadian National, on October 24, 1927, I filed expropriation plans covering property between the tunnel at Lagauchetiere street and the waterfront in the vicinity of Victoria bridge so as to protect the Canadian National against an undue rise in price due to speculative influences in the area which anyone might presume would be the area affected by any possible terminal scheme development. By that time the investigations instituted by Sir Henry Thornton and his advisers had progressed so far as to convince the management of the railway that the site 78594-159
of the tunnel terminal was the most advantageous at which to construct a modern passenger station in which the passenger facilities of the Canadian National railways could be concentrated. It had also become evident to Sir Henry Thornton that the amount of money involved to meet satisfactorily the terminal situation at Montreal was larger even than he had at first anticipated. These views were communicated to me and discussions took place upon the question at that time. In order to make the matter more clear I should point out to the committee that there are at the present time three separate Canadian National stations in the city of Montreal which do not at all directly connect with each other; indeed in one case there is no connection save by going many miles around. That is very inconvenient both for the public and for the operation of the railway.
After discussing the matter on many occasions-and I may say that the management has kept the government through myself, well informed of any developments in that connection-when it became apparent that the problem was so enormous from the point of view of possible financial commitments, while having the utmost faith in the officials of the Canadian National who were particularly charged with the duty of dealing with an engineering enterprise of this character, it was nevertheless thought best both by the government and by the management of the Canadian National railways, and I might add by the engineers of the Canadian National railway staff particularly concerned, to secure if possible some entirely independent outside advice, an outside review, if you will, of all that had been developed in connection with this problem both by the Canadian National engineers and also the eight or nine other proposals which had from time to time been made as tentative solutions of the Montreal terminal problem by various interested parties. In order to obtain this independent advice on the whole terminal question, not only from the standpoint of the Canadian National but also from the standpoint of the interests of the public, the government decided to engage Mr. Frederick Palmer, who was mentioned this afternoon by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, an eminent British engineer who had previously reported on the Hudson Bay terminals, to review and report on the terminal situation in Montreal.
As to Mr. Palmer's qualifications to deal with railway terminal matters, I may tell my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre that Mr. Palmer's initial engineering experience was

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal

in railway work. He has kept up his connection with large railway enterprises from that day until this, and is in fact at the present time still consulting engineer to the government of India in connection with all Indian railway problems. As my hon. friend probably knows, the government of India owns the major part of the Indian railway systems.
Mr. Palmer came to Canada and in due course reviewed the local conditions, physical and traffic, and made a personal study of all the various schemes which had been advanced and to which I referred a moment ago. Eight or nine plans had been advanced by various private interests. The results of the studies which were made by Mr. Palmer have been embodied in his report, dated January 31, 1929, which has been printed and copies of which have been distributed to all Montreal members, and are available also to any member of the house who is interested, and for public distribution. Mr. Palmer in his report states that in his opinion the location development of the Canadian National railway in its studies for a central passenger station is the best which could be thought of not only from the Canadian National standpoint but also from the standpoint of a union terminal to provide for the requirements of both railways should a union terminal be decided upon. That, Mr. Chairman, I believe to be a very important factor, as to whether this proposal of the Canadian National railways would close the door for ever to a union terminal of all the railways in the city of Montreal. Mr. Palmer has studied the situation carefully from that point of view and advances the opinion that the scheme now under consideration, while providing adequately for Canadian National requirements for many years to come, does not close the door to a possible unionizing of all the passenger traffic entering the city of Montreal, should that be decided upon by the parties interested to be in their own best interests and in the interests of the city of Montreal and its people.
That will hardly be accepted.

I am not speaking of
its acceptance; I am referring merely to the question whether this scheme closes the door to a possible union in the future. I would regard it as a matter of some importance if we were at this time closing the door to and thus effectually preventing the development of a union terminal should that be desired in Montreal in the future. I am now merely
[Mr. Dunning.'
advancing the idea, which is confirmed by Mr. Palmer, that the scheme proposed by the Canadian National does not close the door to a possible union in the future.
Not if you have unlimited funds. Anything is possible if you have enough money.

Of course these things do cost money, but I would not follow my hon. friend so far as to say that unlimited money is required. The economic desirability of creating union facilities would, of course, be carefully studied by all the parties who would be required to spend money, and I have no doubt that none of them, the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific, the Montreal Tramways or the city of Montreal, would be prepared to spend the necessary money unless they were convinced from their own point of view, of the economic desirability of doing so.
Mr. Palmer suggested certain modifications in the Canadian National proposal to permit of a more convenient distribution of passengers to and from the passenger terminal and to avoid the congestion of street traffic in the vicinity. He also suggested the development of improved yard facilities accessible to both railways at the west end of the harbour for the purpose of improving the interchange of traffic between the harbour and the railways-a very important factor in the traffic in and around the city and port of Montreal.
With regard to grade separation-and this I think will illustrate the difficulty of that problem for the average member of the house better than anything else I can say-one. of the principal reasons for the complaint on the part of the citizens of Montreal in connection with the Canadian National terminal has been the large number of grade crossings at which there exists an element of danger, and at which delay in the movement of street traffic has been growing. Between Bonaventure station and Victoria bridge and Turcot there are at present 27 grade crossings, some of which are particularly important. Between Moreau street station and the present city limits there are 39 grade crossings. The town of Montreal East and Point aux Trembles contain an additional 9 grade crossings, and on the balance of the line to the east end of the Island at Bout-de-l'Ile, there are, 6 more grade crossings. The total grade crossings are 81. These have always been a source of complaint on the part of the public of Montreal.

With respect to this proposal to expend $50,000,000, I should explain that the bill to be introduced will provide an expenditure of not more than $10,000,000 in any one year, except with special permission by order in council. It is planned to develop the works during the course of the next seven years. I do not expect, neither does the railway management, that during the current fiscal year it will be possible or desirable to spend up to the $10,000,000 which is provided as the yearly limit. As my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre has said, it is difficult in planning works of this magnitude to place any definite limit on what the expenditure will be. My attitude towards engineering estimates for large works is well known. I take a somewhat sceptical view of such estimates. 1 usually regard it as being necessary to allow a proportion over the forecast made by the engineers.

I am not as bad as the lawyers, but the engineers are in that respect, although in some other respects the profession stands very much higher than the legal profession, particularly with respect to the fees charged to the public. The intention, then, is to submit this bill, based upon the resolution, to the general committee of the house on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I have requested the Canadian National railway officials to provide in the railway committee room full detail maps of the whole proposal, and to bring models which they have 78594-159J
prepared, which illustrate graphically what is involved in the entire scheme, and show the city of Montreal and the island of Montreal in miniature. These will enable any member of the committee or of the house to grasp the details in a very short time. When therefore this bill gets before the railway committee I would suggest not only to the members of the committee itself but to all members of the house that they take the opportunity of studying at close range all that is involved in this vast terminal project.
I have only one word more to say. I do hope that when the railway committee is dealing with the matter, if there are interests in the city of Montreal having any constructive views to offer or criticisms of any kind, that they will attend and give the committee the benefit of their advice. As my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre has said, this is one of the largest projects in connection with the Canadian National Railway that we have ever entered upon, and I do hope that all phases of it can be fully developed and fully studied before the committee. I hope the critics, if critics there be, will be present and give us the benefit of their views. The officials of the Canadian National Railway system, who have spent years in studying this project, will be present with all plans, details, and models of what is involved. I know the Canadian National Railway management is desirous, and the government also desires, that the right thing be done in embarking upon an enterprise, so large as this.

Would the minister think it well, not to speak of the plans in detail at the' moment, but to tell the committee something of that part of the scheme which has to do with the development of property in the vicinity of the new terminal? I understand attention has been paid to the development of that part of Montreal, that highways for vehicular and pedestrian traffic have been laid out to suit the station, and I believe there is a plan for util'i7ing the ground purchased but not required for actual railway purposes for warehouses, factories, shops and that sort of thing. speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 71. to

C.N.R.-Purchase oj Alberta Railways
incorporate the Northern Alberta Railways Company, and respecting the Canadian National Railway Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Mir. A. D. M'cRAE (Vancouver North): Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill I give expression to my own personal views only; I feel that the principle art stake merits a further discussion before going into committee.
The residents of the Peace River district, as I found them last fall, were indifferent as to who should be the purchaser of their transportation system so long as the province of Alberta got out of the railway business. 32ither of our two great transcontinental railway systems would be satisfactory to them, but they had some doulbts as to the joint ownership proposed; they feared that the board of directors which will result from the combination, with all the conflicting hopes and ambitions of their principals-agreements bo the contrary notwithstanding-will not make for the rapid development of that new country. They feel certain that in the difference which inevitably will arise the interests of the district will suffer.
I must say that I share their feelings. I can understand our two great railways getting together on joint terminals and perhaps on a main trunk line where density of traffic and cheap ton mileage are the only ends to be considered, but I am sure that a partnership of this kind would not have brought about the present development of the west, which was the work of broad-visioned, courageous men who were in charge of the competing railway companies.
I cannot see that in the joint ownership of the present Alberta railways the interests of pur two railway systems are identical. To begin with, it must be apparent even to the blind that the increasing traffic of the Peace River country cannot long continue over the present railway via Edmonton. Some more direct outlet to the coast must be built, the Canadian Pacific Railway cannot possibly continue to carry its half of the Peace River wheat crop via Calgary to the sea. The Canadian National Railways already have a line to the coast within striking distance of Grande Prairie, but that route is not the natural nutlet for the larger pant of the Peace River district which is north of the Peace river itself.
The economic outlet for this part of the Peace river country is, undoubtedly, by Peace pass, Prince Geoige and Vancouver, and will-
(Mr. Dunning.]
ingly or otherwise that is the outlet which, in the development of that great district, eventually must be constructed.
Why do I say this? Let me give this house a brief description of the country north of the Peace river. Immediately on the west of the Peace river agricultural district, some 150 miles north of Prince George, is the Findlay river mining section, a district already well under development. A few miles east we have a large coal area which Providence has conveniently located at the western door to the Peace river agricultural country, and there is also available nearby, in the Peace River canyon, sufficient water-power to supply cheap power for the entire mining, smelting and refining requirements of that mineral zone. Then, for about 600 miles northeastward to the source of the Mackenzie river, at the northwest end of Great Slave lake, there is a continuous tract of excellent agricultural land.
When we get to the Mackenzie river we are on the doorstep of that now famous precambrian shield which extends across the northern part of the Dominion, the value of which all hon. members fully understand. This shield continues through the Coppermine river mineral reserve to the Arctic, a district which has long promised to be one of the great copper mining areas on the continent. As a matter of fact on the shores of Great Slave lake preparations already are being made for drilling the extensive zinc and lead deposits during the coming summer.
In addition this railway which, we may anticipate, will be joined by a short extension from Peace River Crossing and Edmonton, will meet the Mackenzie river somewhere below Great Slave lake in the vicinity of Fort Providence. When completed it would give a forty-hour rail service from Edmonton to that point as compared with the present infrequent boat journey of eight days down stream and twelve days up stream, and that for a limited time each year. This railway would provide a daily service for twelve months of the year. In fact such a line, by escaping all the boat delays occasioned by ice jams in Great Slave lake, would make it possible to reach the open Mackenzie river six weeks earlier in the spring and leave it two weeks later in the fall, increasing the present season on, the Mackenzie from two and a half months to four and a half months, thus opening up a new Arctic region for this country. The present boat season on the Mackenzie is from July 1 to September 15, but when railway connection is established the Mackenzie river season will be from May

C.N.R.-Purchase of Alberta Railways
15 until early in October. This railway connection would bring into the market via Edmonton the fish of the Great Slave and Great Bear lakes, the Mackenzie river and the Arctic ocean. It would give the mining area to which I have referred a year-round service as against the present limited boat service of two and a half months yearly, under which the country never can develop. Such is the future of this great northern empire when railway facilities are provided.
The unusual attractiveness of this whole railway program is due to the fact that over its entire length from Findlay Forks to Great Slave lake, almost 700 miles, every mile is freight producing and undoubtedly would justify the construction of the line when a definite program for the development of the country is assured.
The Peace pass has been long regarded as the most favourable pass through the Rocky mountains. Undoubtedly there would be some difficulties to contend with in securing acceptable grades; but considering what we have accomplished in that respect already, there need be no fear of eventually not getting the minimum grade necessary for a heavy freight line, which this railway is destined to become, from the Mackenzie river to Vancouver.
From this hurried resume of the district north of the Peace river, I am sure that hon. members will appreciate that there is ample room for both our national railways in that country. I do not believe that this joint proposal is sound. It savours too much of a combination which I am sure will not work out to the benefit of the district.
What does this partnership of our two competing railways actually mean? Does it go any further than the 60 miles of new branch lines provided for in the purchase agreement? Under schedule B, rights, good for five years, are granted to this new combination-provided they start the construction within two years-of four branch lines, totalling approximately 600 milles. At $40,000 per mile this would work out at about $24,000,000, and parliament would have to vote one-half of this amount, or $12,000,000, if these branches are to be built. If this house or either of the railway companies do not feel inclined, because of financial or other reasons, to go ahead, then the branches cannot be built.
It will be observed that this schedule includes the 60 miles the new company is obliged to build under the purchase agreement, so the necessary start is certain to be made. By passing this bill we are tying up for five years the principal branch lines in the Peace River district without any certainty that the construction essential to its development will be proceeded with. It is no assurance of prompt action to say that in case of differences each railway could build its own branches. That is not practical and, therefore, is not probable.
What about the hauling of freight to the sea over the most economical route regardless of who owns it? This is certainly in the interests of the settlers and residents in the Peace River district, and yet this agreement provides for the interests of the companies but not the district.
Are both the railways equally interested in another route through the mountains to the sea? I do not believe they are. As I have already pointed out, the Canadian National system has a line within striking distance of this district. These, and a thousand other equally contentious questions are sure to come before the board of directors representing both of our rival companies.
What about the Peace River country when this new railway partnership does not agree? Where does the district get off at? Is it to stagnate? These are matters which I think the house should consider before giving effect to this legislation. The success of the industries of this country depends upon the continuance of the present healthy competition between our two national railway systems. They are two separate corporations and should always be considered in that way and be treated alike. The joint ownership of the Peace River railways would be the first serious breakdown in this competitive position.
The people of the west might well take heed lest in the precedent about to be established the interests of our two railway systems may in time become so harmonized that this competition, obtained after a waste of so much effort and money, will become a thing of the past.
When speaking about the future railway development in the Peace River district the hon. Minister of Railways said that public opinion would protect the interests of the residents of that district. I have always looked upon public opinion as being a late cure; sometimes too late, and never farsighted, particularly when the development of a new country is concerned.
I cannot see how hon. members from the prairie provinces can support a bill which puts the new settlers of the Peace River district in a position similar to that from which the farmers of Manitoba freed themselves more than a generation ago. Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the merger, even by slow

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hoipe the house will pardon my saying a few words concerning this bill. There is no doubt that this agreement between the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific Railways for the development of the Alberta railway lines was arrived at after considerable care and thought, but I would remind the house of the discussion which arose in 1925 regarding the Peace River country. At that time an estimate was passed to construct an elevator at the port of Prince Rupert, the terminal of the Canadian National lines. If some of the ministers present this evening can remember what they said at that time they will realize that they expressed the view that the building of this elevator and its functioning in the future would become a part and parcel of the development of the Peace River country. It was definitely connected up with the opening of the shortest route to the Pacific coast.
I am opposed to this bill, not because it will be a benefit to Alberta but on the ground that it will materially interfere with the opening up of the legitimate, natural outlet for the Peace River country. I think that is the most important aspect of this matter. The hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. McRae) has summed up very well the difficulties which must be met. The Canadian National Railways should carry out what I consider to be a moral obligation on their part to protect and guard their own line to the port of Prince Rupert.
I do not think it would be advisable at this time for me to say where the outlet from the Peace River should go to, nor do I believe it is possible for anyone to say that. During the past three years we have had many reports from the engineers of both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways, Four passes, Obed, Monkman, Pine and Peace river, were mentioned. I contend that in no instance have we been able definitely to say where the proper economic outlet to the Peace River district should be. It may be known to the Canadian National, or the Canadian Pacific, or to the engineers of both these great railway systems, but I honestly believe that this is where the Canadian National failed. The Peace River country is really a district that the Canadian National. should have taken the utmost interest in. What has happened? We must acknowledge facts as we see them. I hope the Min-
[Mr McRae.]
ister, of Railways will not be offended, but I believe the Canadian National have been negligent in the duty which devolved upon them in not taking over for themselves the development of the Peace River country. The Canadian Pacific entered the field; they sent in their engineers repeatedly, and finally- they were prior to the Canadian National so far as I am aware

they decided that they were going to develop that country. Then it was that the Canadian National entered.
A few weeks ago I asked the minister whether he believed that this agreement would interfere with, retard or hasten the development of an outlet from the Peace River district to the Pacific coast, and he replied that he believed it would facilitate it. I do not believe that it can facilitate the development of the nearest economic route to the Pacific ocean for this reason: Can anyone say that either of these two great railway companies, working on a fifty-fifty basis, can break away from this contract and start in to feed their own lines irrespective of the other? I do not know how this can be done. I believe both railway companies have agreed to a survey along the Pacific Great Eastern. If that survey is satisfactory and if it meets the requirements as regards possibilities of freight, these companies will be obligated to connect up with the Pacific Great Eastern say from Prince George. If that be the case -and it is a possibility-I say to the Minister of Railways: It is futile to think that the Canadian National port of Prince Rupert will benefit in the least degree from that. If Prince George is connected with the Pacific Great Eastern, undoubtedly, geographically the only way whereby freight from the Peace River district will flow in accord with that railway development, will be down that line.

If the Pacific Great Eastern is found acceptable-and both companies have agreed to make a survey of it-and if it were understood, according to the hon. member for North Vancouver, that from Grand Prairie a line would be built to Prince George, I contend that the Canadian National line to the port of Prince Rupert would be left practically high and dry. I ask the Minister of Railways to consider this seriously. One of two things should be done regarding the national line to the port of Prince Rupert. One is that steps should be taken to connect

C.N.R.-Purchase oj Alberta Railways
up their branch lines in Alberta with some point on the Canadian National west of Prince George, so as to ensure that the port of Prince Rupert and the line of the Canadian National will receive a portion of freight developed, or let the Canadian Pacific take over the line. What do we find today? Anybody who has read the wheat records of the past week must realize that a great change has taken place regarding the movement of wheat to the various world ports. We find that the Argentine and Australia are now big competitors with Canada in the matter of wheat. The reason is obvious, namely, that their wheat moves when our wheat is lying in cold storage, in the elevators on the great lakes. The result is that we must turn more and more to the movement of wheat to the Pacific coast. Vancouver has received so far over 80,000,000 bushels of wheat and no doubt she will receive more. The reason is that the port is open for twelve months in the year. The port of Prince Rupert is likewise open for twelve months in' the year and it is nearer to the Orient than any other port on the Pacific coast. It is 480 miles nearer to five big ports in the Orient, for instance, Kobe, Shanghai, Tokyo and others. That being the case, the people of Prince Rupert look upon this development in Alberta with very grave fears; they are afraid that it means the holding up of rightful development or a great delay in the matter of bringing a share of the produce from the Peace River district to the port of Prince Rupert. I believe there is plenty of room for Stewart, Prince Rupert and Vancouver to share in this development; I do not believe the grain will flow through one main channel; it will break up and divide into these three channels if the opportunity is afforded. I trust therefore that the Minister of Railways will satisfy us regarding the future of the port of Prince Rupert. We have a large ocean dock there; we have also an elevator that has been closed throughout the year, and I am sorry to say-but this is the place to say these things; after all, it is the only place where a man can determine whether he has facts or not-that I have it on good authority that last season's shipments of wheat destined for the port of Prince Rupert were changed at Jasper and deflected to the port of Vancouver. I should like to know on whose authority or why that deflection took place. There must be a good reason for it and as the port of Prince Rupert is a national creation, the people expect that at least it shall receive some attention in the big development that is going on and will go on
in the Peace River country. I do think that some clause should be placed in this bill to assure the people of western Canada that there shall be no interference with any extension which the Canadian National might make towards joining up their own line to the port of Prince Rupert, and I would like the Minister of Railways before this bill is sent to the committee to enlighten us as to what he considers the situation will be should this bill pass. I have read the bill carefully and I find that first of all three conditions must be met, and that practically immediately the bill becomes law. Then there are other conditions which are introduced with the word " may," such as, "The company may construct and operate one hundred and two miles," and so on. In other words, they do not need to enter upon that work at all; they "may" do it. Therefore I think we are entitled to be satisfied that the future of the port of Prince Rupert is not in danger and that that port will not be overlooked.
I would just like to draw attention to another feature. The other evening the minister mentioned that certain existing lines in eastern Canada were to be taken over by the Canadian National at a sum running up to about $10,000,000. We have the great Hudson Bay railway on our hands, and I do not think that anybody in this house or anyone in Canada can say definitely that that great engineering work is going to be a success. These will involve heavy responsibilities financially. The Hudson Bay railway is still a theoretical proposition; there is no guarantee that it will fulfil the requirements, and that it will function in accordance with our expectations. The Peace River development will benefit all Canada.
There is one other thing which I think cannot be denied and that is that the Canadian National has in the port of Prince Rupert a port second to none strategically, and second to none as a port itself, because there is no expense attached to it. It is looked upon by ocean captains as one of the finest harbours on the whole coast of America. Therefore I do not think that I am trespassing upon the time of the house when I request the Minister of Railways to see that the Canadian National safeguard the interests of that port and maintain the line running to .Prince Rupert in their own system and make it function, in order to build up the port of Prince Rupert, instead of concentrating the whole movement of grain and all other produce on the line down to the port of Vancouver. I do not think that that is the best think to do either nationally or

Mr. Speaker, I wish to record in a general way my support of the proposed legislation now before the house. I am not going to say that I am absolutely satisfied with its provisions, I am one of those who have laboured for some time to persuade the government and the Canadian National Railways to act in connection with this matter, both as to the taking over of the Peace river section of the Alberta railways and the construction of a railway out to the Pacific coast. I have declared in Alberta as well as here my disappointment that some provision was not made in connection with the coast outlet. However, to oppose the bill does not, as I see it, get us anywhere nearer a Pacific coast outlet than to allow it to pass; in fact it is just the reverse, in my judgment. I think it has been recognized in all our discussions of this question that one of the chief difficulties in connection with a coast outlet was simply the fact that the Edmonton Dunvegan and the Central Canada Railways which would be part of the system to connect the Peace River country with the Pacific coast, belonged to the province of Alberlta, and it was not expected by anyone in that province or outside of it, so far as I know, that Alberta would build a railway through British Columbia to any Pacific coast port.
Now, to oppose this bill, as I understand it, would simply mean that the Canadian Pacific Railway would get the Alberta railways. It may be that some hon. members, as well as certain people outside this house 'believe that that would ensure the best development of the Peace River country. But I am not convinced of that. I am not insensible to the possible difficulties in connection with the working out of this legislation, that were referred to to-night by the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. McRae); but when it ooroes to the question of the Objection he raised, as I understood him, to the House of Commons, possibly not being ready to vote $12,000,000 to build its share of the 600 miles of branch lines for which this railway company will hold charters in the Peace River country, I think it more likely that parliament would provide that $12,000,000, than that we would carry out the program referred to in the correspondence which was brought down yesterday. I find that on September 20th, i92S, Sir Henry Thornton wired the Minister of Railways as follows:
Canadian Press announce Canadian Pacific has made independent offer something less than twenty-five million for Alberta Government Railways and receipt of offer acknowledged by Brownlee Montreal urgently suggest and 1 agree we should announce we propose ask parliamentary authority build line Obed through Grand Prairie northwesterly towards Peace or Pine pass with branch from Sturgeon lake northeasterly towards McLennan and Peace river crossing. Kindly telegraph quickly your views.
Thornton.
That expenditure would not open up anything like the vast area of new territory that the 600 miles would open up, and yet it would cost, not $12,000,000, but possibly $20,000,000 or S30.000.000, if we are to go by the experience in the province of Alberta, and I think they built their mileage just as cheaply as the Canadian National Railways. If that is the only alternative to joint ownership, I would rather wrestle with the problem of joint ownership of the present railways and the problem of future development in the extending of branch lines, because I do not believe this parliament would be likely to vote money for the duplication practically of the present railway without serving any very large amount of new territory.
During the last three or four years the Peace River country has been very, very anxious to see the Canadian National Railways take over the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway. I find also that the Alberta government was very anxious that the Canadian National Railways should buy the Alberta railways, and two years ago, May 3, 1926, according to sessional paper 226A of 1928, I find an offer by the Premier of Alberta, Mr. Brownlee, to the Minister of Railways, Mr. Dunning, in which he argues for the taking over of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway and the Central Canada Railway at a price just a little over $14,000,000. These figures were submitted, not as a final offer, but as a basis for consideration. I may say that the price agreed to be paid for the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway by the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific must be $20,000,000. Probably I should read one or two paragraphs of this letter:
Dear Mr. Dunning,

In submitting, for your consideration, the proposition that the Canadian National Railways should take over the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway and the Central Canada Railway, I desire to draw your attention to the following:'-[DOT]
1.	The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, between Wolf Creek and Prince Rupert, was constructed at a very heavy cost as a main artery to serve the country which is tributary to it, and, as this portion of the national railway system is short on traffic, the loss on operation, maintenance, and interest on capital represents a large proportion of the annual deficit on the national railway system. The mileage between the above points is 834.3 and, at $125,000 per mile, which is a fair estimate of the cost at the present time, amounts to $104,287,500 capital investment. If the Peace River territory is not obtained as a feeder for this main artery, it will preclude any possibility of the traffic necessary to provide revenues sufficient .to carry the interest on this capital investment.
2.	The Edmonton. Dunvegan and British Columbia and Central Canada railways tap the productive portion of the Peace River territory which has been developed up to the present time, and are a valuable addition to any railway system which assumes the responsibility for the future development of that country. These railways were built as colonization lines and, as such, should have received a subsidy from the Dominion government: in fact, 50 miles between Roycroft junction and Grande Prairie on the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia was subsidized to the amount of $6,400 per mile, and $175,000 was paid to assist in the construction of the bridge across Peace river on the Central Canada railway, which sets out clearly the fact that the Dominion government did partially recognize their responsibility in this respect.

3.	The traffic which these lines provide will justify their purchase by the national system, as, under present conditions, the profits on the traffic will almost meet the interest on the capital to be assumed in addition to taking care of the cost of operation and maintenance, and with the future development and settlement of that vast territory will become very valuable to the system as the years go on.
4.	The Peace River tract of land in northern British Columbia, which is owned by the crown in the right of the Dominion, contains 3,500.000 acres, 1,200,000 acres of which is reported to be good agricultural land and through which the proposed western outlet for the Peace River would pass; if sold it would provide a large portion of the cost of construction to connect the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia with the national railway at Prince George.
5.	For the above reasons it is submitted that the interests of the taxpayers of the Dominion of Canada will be served by obtaining the Peace River territory as a feeder to the Canadian National system.

I have handed you a memorandum showing that a fair valuation of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia and Central Canada railways is approximately $17,472,994.43. Against this, the province has guaranteed debentures totalling $9,420,000, payable in thirty years from the date of issue, and has advanced other sums, from time to time with proper security, totalling $9,388,456.93, making a total claim, as at December 31st, 1925, of approximately $18,808,456.93.
As a basis for consideration, it is suggested that the Dominion government should:
(a)	Assume the liability for payment of the said guaranteed bonds, amounting to $9,420,009.
(b)	Issue debentures or other security, pay-.able on such terms as may be agreed, for 50 per
cent of the amount advanced by the province ($9,388,456.93) as above $4,694,228.47.
I have informed you orally of the nature of the security held by the Royal Bank of Canada, totalling $2,400,000, with accrued interest, and the terms of settlement already suggested. We propose the Dominion government should assume this obligation in addition to the above.
Yours very truly,
J. E. Brownlee.
Honourable C. A. Dunning,
Minister of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa.
